newsitem.title: UK: Stargazers ponder "missing" U.S. spy satellites.
newsitem.headline: Stargazers ponder "missing" U.S. spy satellites.

text.p: Four U.S. spy satellites "missing" since 1990 may have been moved into secret orbits so they could carry on their covert duties without being tracked, the New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.

The mysterious disappearances have been noticed by a small band of enthusiasts whose hobby is tracking satellites by monitoring their positions in the night sky and then using a computer to reconstruct their orbits.

Ted Molczan, a satellite spotter in Toronto monitored three of the satellites from the time of their launch from Vandenberg Air Force Base in California in 1990 and noticed they all disappeared after several weeks in their initial orbits.
"It left the orbit," he said. "It was there for a while and then it disappeared."
So far, no one has been able to track any of the missing satellites in their presumed orbits and their whereabouts remain unknown to everyone outside of the U.S. intelligence agencies.

Satellite watchers do not rule out the possibility that the satellites could have stopped working and been deliberately destroyed. But Molczan said this was unlikely, as dead U.S. spy satellites are usually left in orbit.
John Pike, a space analyst with the Washington D.C.-based Federation of American Scientists noted that one of the satellites diappeared just before the Gulf War.
If the satellite had died, the failure would have produced howls of protest from members of Congress who monitor U.S. intelligence gathering - something that did not happen, he said.

A more intriguing possibility is that the satellites were placed into orbits which would move more slowly across the skies than other high-altitude snoopers, giving them more time to photograph targets.

Supporters of this theory point to the timing of the U.S. air strikes in Iraq last September. Military strikes are usually mounted immediately before a spy satellite passes overhead, so that they can record the damage before the enemy has time to cover it up.

But after the latest strikes in early September, when the U.S launched cruise missiles as punishment for Iraqi attacks on northern Iraqi Kurds, no known spy satellites would have passed over the target area for between two and six hours.
This suggests that one or more of the missing satellites may have been watching, satellite watchers said.
